Our first NLP problem: Language Modelling
What is the probability of a given sequence of words in a particular
language (e.g. English)?
Odd problem. Applications?
[Slide 8]
Applications of LMs
Word likelihood for query completion in information retrieval
(“Is Manchester”→try it on your search engine)
Grammatical error detection (“You’re welcome” or “Your
welcome”?)
Speech recognition (“I scream is delicious.” or “Ice cream is
delicious.”?)
[Slide 9]
Traditional AI approach
Look for interpretation which is
grammatical
semantically sensible
pragmatically plausible in context
Build explicit models of rules describing how language works
Poor performance in real world
hard to maintain wide-coverage systems
too much knowledge needed for semantics
[Slide 10]
Statistical Approaches
No explicit models of grammar, meaning, context, etc.
Instead, collect statistics such as
how often different words appear
how often pairs (or triples, etc.) of words appear next to each
other

Statistical Approaches
No explicit models of grammar, meaning, context, etc.
Instead, collect statistics such as
how often different words appear
how often pairs (or triples, etc.) of words appear next to each
other
Or other more complex statistical patterns
Use this statistics to perform NLP tasks
speech, text prediction, translation, ...
[Slide 11]
N-gram Statistics
See how often word(s) occur
single words (unigram)
word pairs (bigram)
word triples (trigram)
Assign a probability to each sequence interpretation, using the
statistics
Pick highest-probability one
[Slide 12]
Language Models
N-gram models: probabilistic models that predict the next
word from the previousN−1 words
Such statistical models of word sequences are also called
language models(LMs).

Intrinsic Evaluation: Accuracy
How well does our LM predict the next word?
I always order pizza with cheese and...
mushrooms?
bread?
and?
Accuracy: how often the LM predicts the correct word
The higher the better
[Slide 43]

Perplexity: measures the ability of the model to predict word
of an unseen text
Unseen = not in training data, e.g., test set
The average negative log-likelihood of the test set
x= [x 1, ...,xN ], normalised by the number of wordsN.

Add-1 Smoothing
Add-1 (or Laplace) smoothing adds one to all counts:
PAdd−1 (xn) = c(x n) + 1

Add-k Smoothing
Add-1 puts too much probability mass to unseen words, better to
add-k,k<1:
PAdd−k (xn) = counts(x n) +k

kis a hyperparameter: choose optimal value on the dev set!
